title: 21-Step System Design Interview Framework
description: Master the battle-tested 21-step structured interview framework used to consistently ace Senior and Staff System Design interviews at FAANG and top-tier tech companies. Break down ambiguous problem statements, drive proactive live clarification, perform mental back-of-the-envelope capacity estimations, draw multi-tier architectural block diagrams, define precise API contracts, model resilient database schemas, and defend trade-offs under pressure.

topics.title: The 21-Step Battle-Tested System Design Interview Process
topics.definition: The 21-Step System Design Interview Framework is an end-to-end, time-managed communication and architectural methodology designed to guide a candidate through a 45-minute technical system design interview. Rather than randomly drawing boxes or rushing into database choices, the candidate systematically guides the conversation across four distinct phases: Scoping & Clarification (0-10m), High-Level Architecture (10-25m), Deep Dive & Component Design (25-38m), and Scaling, Bottlenecks & Trade-off Defense (38-45m).
topics.why_we_need_it:
In high-stakes system design interviews, 80% of candidates fail not because of a lack of technical knowledge, but because of chaotic communication: jumping straight into drawing database tables without scoping requirements, designing for 1,000 QPS when the interviewer expects 100,000 QPS, or monopolizing the whiteboard without validating interviewer alignment.

Interviewers grade candidates on four core competencies: (1) Navigating Ambiguity; (2) Quantitative Systems Engineering (Capacity Math); (3) Architectural Breadth and Depth; (4) Trade-off Defense and Failure Mode Resilience. A structured framework guarantees you cover all grading rubric criteria within the 45-minute window.
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine a master trial attorney presenting a complex corporate litigation case to a jury. The attorney doesn't burst into the courtroom shouting random evidence. They deliver a clear opening statement outlining the case scope (Scoping), present the physical timeline and core exhibits (High-Level Architecture), call expert witnesses to dissect technical forensic details (Deep Dive), and anticipate the opposing counsel's cross-examination objections before concluding (Bottlenecks and Trade-offs).
topics.how_it_works:
The 21 steps are executed across four strict time-boxed phases:

  1. Phase 1: Requirements Scoping & Estimations (0 - 10 Mins):
    • Step 1: Understand the problem & clarify business goals.
    • Step 2: Establish 3-4 Core Functional Requirements.
    • Step 3: Clarify Out-of-Scope features explicitly.
    • Step 4: Define Non-Functional Requirements (Latency, Availability, Consistency).
    • Step 5: Perform Back-of-the-Envelope Traffic Math (QPS, Peak QPS).
    • Step 6: Perform Storage, Bandwidth & Cache Memory Estimations.
  2. Phase 2: High-Level Architecture & API Design (10 - 25 Mins):
    • Step 7: Define Core REST / gRPC API Contracts.
    • Step 8: Design Data Model & Database Schema (Entities, Keys).
    • Step 9: SQL vs NoSQL Storage Technology Selection Justification.
    • Step 10: Draw the High-Level End-to-End Block Diagram.
    • Step 11: Walk through the Core Happy-Path User Flow.
    • Step 12: Proactively pause and calibrate with the interviewer.
  3. Phase 3: Deep-Dive Component Engineering (25 - 38 Mins):
    • Step 13: Deep-dive into the primary technical choke point.
    • Step 14: Data Partitioning & Sharding Strategy (Shard Key).
    • Step 15: Caching Strategy & Invalidation Policies.
    • Step 16: Message Queuing & Asynchronous Decoupling.
    • Step 17: Idempotency & Concurrency Race Condition Elimination.
  4. Phase 4: Resiliency, Trade-offs & Wrap-Up (38 - 45 Mins):
    • Step 18: Single Point of Failure (SPOF) Analysis.
    • Step 19: Disaster Recovery, Multi-AZ & Replication Lag Defense.
    • Step 20: Quantitative Trade-off Matrix Summary.
    • Step 21: Summarize future optimizations and conclude cleanly.

conceptual_breakdown.explanation: Allocate strictly 10 minutes to scoping, 15 minutes to high-level architecture, 13 minutes to deep dives, and 7 minutes to failure modes. Running out of time before reaching deep dives is an instant fail signal.
Never talk for more than 3 minutes without calibrating: 'Does this high-level architecture align with what you'd like to focus on, or should we dive into the data sharding strategy next?'
Senior candidates drive the conversation proactively like a Tech Lead running an RFC architecture review, rather than passively waiting for the interviewer to prompt every step.

There are no silver bullets in system design, only trade-offs. Stating 'We will use Cassandra because it is fast' is weak; stating 'We choose Cassandra over PostgreSQL because we need horizontal write scalability and can tolerate eventual consistency for user comments' is Staff-level.

rows: Jumps straight to drawing boxes; assumes requirements
Spends 5-8 mins asking probing questions; defines boundaries
Skips math or does inaccurate calculations
Estimates QPS, storage, and cache memory cleanly with round numbers
Evaluates access patterns, ACID needs, and query shapes objectively
Monologues for 15 minutes; defensive on pushback
Collaborative partner; welcomes feedback and pivots gracefully
Proactively identifies network partitions, crashes, and mitigation

tradeoffs.analysis: Covering the full end-to-end architecture (Breadth) is required first before plunging into deep technical details (Depth). Going deep too early risks missing core requirements.
Do not waste time calculating $86,400 \times 365$ precisely. Round 1 day to $100,000$ seconds or $86,400 \approx 86k$ to keep mental calculations rapid and error-free.

failure_scenarios.impact: Interviewer says: 'Now assume 10% of users are celebrities with 100M followers.'
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Do not panic. Acknowledge the bottleneck calmly: 'That introduces the Celebrity Fan-out problem. Let me adapt our push model to a hybrid push-pull architecture.'

failure_scenarios.scenario: Running Out of Time at 35-Minute Mark with No Scaling Discussion
failure_scenarios.impact: Interviewer cuts you off without seeing scaling depth.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Accelerate Phase 2: quickly outline remaining boxes and explicitly say: 'Now let's dive into the scaling bottlenecks and fault tolerance.'

common_mistakes.mistake: Designing an entire system without asking clarifying questions
common_mistakes.correction: Treat the opening prompt as an intentionally ambiguous scenario. Always clarify active users, write/read ratios, and out-of-scope boundaries.

common_mistakes.mistake: Claiming a system is '100% Consistent and 100% Available' (Violating CAP)
common_mistakes.correction: Demonstrates a lack of distributed systems fundamentals. Always state your CAP trade-off clearly (CP vs AP) based on business context.

interview_questions.question: What is the single most important rule during the first 5 minutes of a System Design interview?
interview_questions.answer: Clarify the problem scope and establish non-negotiable boundaries. System design prompts (e.g., 'Design YouTube') are deliberately massive and impossible to solve in 45 minutes. The candidate must proactively lead the scoping: establish 2-3 core functional use cases, explicitly declare out-of-scope features (e.g., 'We will focus strictly on video upload and adaptive streaming; comments, recommendations, and monetization are out of scope'), and agree on scale metrics (DAU, write/read ratios) before drawing a single box.

interview_questions.question: How do you handle an interviewer challenging your architectural decision (e.g., 'Why not use MongoDB instead of PostgreSQL here?')?
interview_questions.answer: Never become defensive or dismissive. Frame your response using structured trade-off analysis: (1) Acknowledge the validity of their suggestion ('MongoDB is a great option for flexible document schemas and horizontal sharding'); (2) State the specific business requirement driving your original choice ('However, for this payment ledger service, we require strict multi-row ACID transactions and relational foreign-key integrity to prevent financial balance drift'); (3) Conclude with the boundary condition ('If our write throughput exceeded a single primary's IOPS and we relaxed ACID to eventual consistency, MongoDB with sharding would be the superior choice').

topics.title: Steps 1-6: Live Clarification, User Flow & Estimation Calculations
topics.definition: Steps 1 through 6 form Phase 1 of the System Design interview, where the candidate takes full command of problem ambiguity, defines explicit functional and non-functional requirements, outlines primary user personas and interaction flows, and performs rapid back-of-the-envelope capacity calculations (QPS, Peak QPS, Storage per Year, Bandwidth Egress, and Cache Memory).
topics.why_we_need_it: Without quantitative estimation, architectural decisions are arbitrary. Designing a cache tier for 50 QPS is an over-engineering anti-pattern; failing to design a cache tier for 50,000 QPS will crash your database. Back-of-the-envelope calculations provide the mathematical justification for every subsequent architectural component (load balancers, sharded databases, CDNs, Redis clusters).
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine an aerospace structural engineer designing a suspension bridge. Before drawing blueprints or ordering steel beams, the engineer calculates: 'How many vehicles cross per hour? What is the maximum wind load during a hurricane? What is the total static tonnage?' Drawing blueprints without load math guarantees the bridge collapses.
topics.how_it_works:
Executing Steps 1 to 6 with mathematical precision:

  1. Step 1: Clarifying Questions: Ask targeted boundary questions: 'Are we designing for global mobile clients?' 'Do we need real-time sync or is 5-second eventual consistency acceptable?'
  2. Step 2: Functional Requirements (Pick 3-4): Write clear bullets: (1) User can create short URL; (2) User is redirected to target URL; (3) User views analytics.
  3. Step 3: Non-Functional Requirements: (1) High Availability ($99.99\%$); (2) Low Latency ($<20$ms redirect); (3) Read-heavy (100:1).
  4. Step 4: The 24-Hour Math Cheat Sheet: Remember: 1 Day = $86,400 \text{ seconds} \approx 100,000 \text{ seconds}$. 1 Million requests/day $= \frac{1,000,000}{100,000} = 10 \text{ requests/sec}$. 1 Billion requests/day $= 10,000 \text{ requests/sec}$.
  5. Step 5: QPS & Peak QPS Calculation: If system has 100M Daily Active Users (DAU) making 10 requests/day $= 1\text{B requests/day} \approx 10,000 \text{ QPS average}$. Peak QPS $= 2 \times \text{Average} = 20,000 \text{ QPS}$.
  6. Step 6: Storage & Cache Sizing (Pareto 80/20 Rule): (a) Storage: $10M \text{ writes/day} \times 1\text{KB} \times 365 = 3.65 \text{ TB/year}$; (b) Cache: Cache 20% of daily read volume: $1\text{B reads} \times 0.20 \times 1\text{KB} = 200 \text{ GB RAM}$.

conceptual_breakdown.concept: The Power of Two Units Cheat Sheet
Latency Numbers Every Engineer Should Know (Jeff Dean)
conceptual_breakdown.explanation: L1 Cache: 0.5ns; RAM Access: 100ns; NVMe SSD Read: 10-50µs; Same Datacenter RTT: 0.5ms; Cross-US Fiber RTT: 50-100ms; Trans-Atlantic RTT: 150ms.
Traffic is not evenly distributed across 24 hours. Diurnal traffic spikes typically hit $2\times$ to $3\times$ average QPS. Always size compute and load balancers for Peak QPS.
$\text{Egress Bandwidth} = \text{Read QPS} \times \text{Average Payload Size}$. For 10,000 QPS at 50KB payload $= 500 \text{ MB/s} = 4 \text{ Gbps}$ egress network interface requirement.

tradeoffs.analysis: Do not get bogged down in multi-decimal arithmetic. Rounding numbers (e.g., $86,400 \rightarrow 100,000$) allows you to complete all calculations in under 2 minutes, preserving time for architecture.

Estimating for $5\times$ peak ensures 100% uptime during extreme flash sales, but triples cloud infrastructure cost. Sizing for $2\times$ peak paired with Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) balances safety and cost.

failure_scenarios.scenario: Arithmetic Unit Error (Confusing Bytes and Bits)
failure_scenarios.impact: Candidate writes 500 MB/s as 500 Mbps, underestimating network bandwidth by 8x.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Remember: 1 Byte ($B$) = 8 bits ($b$). Bandwidth is quoted in bits per second (Gbps); storage and memory in Bytes (GB).

failure_scenarios.impact: Interviewer asks: 'How many Redis nodes do we need?' and candidate has no memory estimation ready.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Always calculate 20% of daily read volume as your baseline Redis cluster memory requirement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Spending 15 minutes calculating exact decimal math
common_mistakes.correction: Round aggressively. The interviewer cares about your quantitative reasoning and order-of-magnitude estimates ($10^3, 10^6, 10^9$), not mental calculator precision.

common_mistakes.mistake: Designing for 100 million users without checking if the prompt was for an internal corporate tool (10k users)
common_mistakes.correction: Always ask: 'Are we building for public internet scale (100M users) or an enterprise internal tool (10k users)?'

interview_questions.question: How do you quickly estimate QPS and storage for a system with 50 million Daily Active Users?
interview_questions.answer: Use standard mental rounding: (1) **QPS:** Assume each user makes 10 requests/day $\rightarrow 50M \times 10 = 500M$ requests/day. Divide by $100,000$ seconds/day $\rightarrow 5,000$ Average QPS. Peak QPS $= 2 \times 5,000 = 10,000$ QPS; (2) **Storage:** If 10% of requests are writes (50M writes/day) with 2KB payload: $50M \times 2\text{KB} = 100\text{ GB/day}$. Annual Storage $= 100\text{GB} \times 365 \approx 36.5 \text{ TB/year}$; (3) **Cache:** 20% daily read volume $= 450M \times 0.20 \times 2\text{KB} = 180 \text{ GB RAM}$ for Redis.

interview_questions.question: Why is Jeff Dean's 'Latency Numbers Every Computer Scientist Should Know' important in a System Design interview?
interview_questions.answer: These numbers provide physical reality checks for architectural trade-offs: (1) L1/L2 cache ($0.5-5$ns) and Main Memory RAM access (~100ns) are 10,000x faster than reading from NVMe SSD flash ($50-100$µs), proving why in-memory caching is mandatory for high QPS; (2) Data center local network round-trip ($0.5$ms) is 200x faster than cross-ocean fiber ($150$ms), proving why multi-region active-active architectures cannot use synchronous cross-region database replication.

topics.title: Steps 7-12: Live High-Level Block Diagram, DB & API Contracts
topics.definition: Steps 7 through 12 form Phase 2 of the interview, translating scoped requirements into concrete technical abstractions: defining clean REST/gRPC API signatures, designing normalized/denormalized database schemas with partition keys, objectively justifying SQL vs NoSQL technology selection, and drawing a clean end-to-end multi-tier architectural block diagram.
topics.why_we_need_it: A system design interview cannot remain abstract prose. The high-level block diagram establishes the structural blueprint of your distributed system. Drawing clean, decoupled components (Client, CDN, API Gateway, Stateless Services, Cache, Message Queues, Sharded Databases) allows both you and the interviewer to visualize data flow, identify bottlenecks, and anchor subsequent deep-dive discussions.
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine an architectural blueprint for a skyscraper. Before picking out carpet colors or bathroom tiles, the lead architect draws the structural skeleton: foundation pilings, steel load-bearing columns, elevator shafts, electrical conduits, and water main inputs. Every contractor refers to this master blueprint throughout construction.
topics.how_it_works:
Executing Steps 7 to 12 systematically:

  1. Step 7: Define API Contracts: Write concise, production-ready endpoint signatures: 
    POST /v1/tweets
Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>, Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
Request: {"text": "Hello world", "media_ids": ["m102"]}
Response: 201 Created {"tweet_id": "tw-9841", "created_at": 1730000000}
  2. Step 8: Database Schema Design: Define primary entities, column data types, foreign keys, and primary indexes: users(user_id PK, email, created_at), tweets(tweet_id PK, author_id, text, media_urls, created_at).
  3. Step 9: Storage Selection Justification: Defend SQL vs NoSQL based on access patterns: (a) Choose Relational SQL (Postgres/MySQL) if relational joins, strong ACID consistency, and structured queries dominate; (b) Choose NoSQL (Cassandra/DynamoDB) if massive horizontal write throughput, dynamic schemas, and simple key-value/partition lookups dominate.
  4. Step 10: Draw the End-to-End Block Diagram: Connect Clients $\rightarrow$ Route 53 DNS $\rightarrow$ CDN $\rightarrow$ API Gateway (Auth & Rate Limit) $\rightarrow$ Stateless App Service $\rightarrow$ Redis Cache $\rightarrow$ Database Cluster + Async Kafka Worker Pipeline.
  5. Step 11: End-to-End Flow Trace: Walk through a complete write and read transaction trace across every box.
  6. Step 12: Interviewer Alignment Check: 'Now that our high-level architecture is established, which component should we deep-dive into?'

conceptual_breakdown.explanation: Including `Idempotency-Key: <UUID>` in all state-modifying POST requests ensures network retries never cause duplicate payments or entity creation.
In distributed NoSQL, the Partition Key determines which physical server holds the data; the Sort Key determines chronological ordering on disk.
Never store session memory or files on the API server. Keep servers 100% stateless so any node can service any incoming request behind the load balancer.
Move slow operations (notifications, indexing, video transcoding) out of synchronous HTTP request paths into Kafka/RabbitMQ queues.

rows: Typed table schema with dynamic clustering keys

tradeoffs.factor: REST vs gRPC for Internal Services
tradeoffs.analysis: REST/JSON is universal and human-readable for public client APIs. gRPC over HTTP/2 with binary Protobuf is 5x-10x faster and strictly typed, making it the ideal standard for internal microservice-to-microservice calls.

Normalized relational models prevent data duplication and guarantee consistency, but require expensive SQL joins. Denormalized NoSQL models duplicate data to achieve ultra-fast single-partition reads.

failure_scenarios.scenario: Drawing a Single Database Box for 100,000 Write QPS
failure_scenarios.impact: Interviewer points out a single database primary maxes out at ~10,000 writes/sec.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Immediately introduce Database Sharding with a clear Shard Key or adopt a distributed NoSQL engine (Cassandra/DynamoDB).

failure_scenarios.scenario: Forgetting Rate Limiting on Public API Gateway
failure_scenarios.impact: System is vulnerable to DDoS attacks and scraping.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Add a distributed Token Bucket rate limiter at the API Gateway layer using Redis.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing arrows between boxes without labeling protocols or payloads
common_mistakes.correction: Always label every architectural arrow: write 'HTTPS / REST', 'gRPC', 'Async Kafka Topic', or 'Cache Check (<1ms)'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Claiming NoSQL is always better than SQL for scale
common_mistakes.correction: Relational databases like PostgreSQL easily handle 50,000+ read QPS with read replicas and caching. Always justify database choice based on query shapes and ACID requirements.

interview_questions.question: How do you decide between SQL and NoSQL in a System Design interview?
interview_questions.answer: Evaluate four concrete criteria: (1) **Data Structure & Access Pattern:** If data is highly relational with complex multi-table joins (e.g., financial transactions, ERP systems), choose **Relational SQL**. If data is simple key-value, document, or time-series accessed by single partition keys without joins, choose **NoSQL**; (2) **ACID vs Eventual Consistency:** Choose SQL for strict financial multi-row transactions; choose NoSQL (Cassandra/DynamoDB) if eventual consistency is acceptable; (3) **Write Scalability:** A single SQL primary caps out around 10k-20k writes/sec before requiring manual sharding; NoSQL scales writes horizontally by adding nodes; (4) **Schema Evolution:** Choose SQL for stable schemas; NoSQL for rapidly changing unstructured JSON payloads.

interview_questions.question: What is the role of an API Gateway in a microservices architecture?
interview_questions.answer: An API Gateway acts as the single entry point (reverse proxy) for all external client traffic. It centralizes cross-cutting concerns: (1) **Authentication & Authorization:** Validates JWT/OAuth tokens before requests hit internal services; (2) **SSL/TLS Termination:** Offloads heavy cryptographic decryption from internal compute nodes; (3) **Rate Limiting & DDoS Defense:** Enforces token bucket limits per IP/User; (4) **Request Routing & Aggregation:** Routes `/orders/*` to Order Service and aggregates multiple microservice calls into a single response; (5) **Protocol Translation:** Translates public HTTP/REST requests to internal high-speed gRPC/Protobuf calls.

topics.title: Steps 13-21: Scaling Bottlenecks, Failure Defense & Trade-offs
topics.definition: Steps 13 through 21 represent the final, decisive Phase of the interview where Senior and Staff engineers separate themselves. In this phase, the candidate dives deep into domain-specific choke points, eliminates Single Points of Failure (SPOFs), designs database sharding and caching policies, handles race conditions with idempotency and distributed locking, and summarizes the master Trade-off Matrix.
topics.why_we_need_it: Any junior engineer can draw a generic three-tier diagram (Load Balancer -> App -> DB). High-level interviews are won or lost in the **Deep Dive and Failure Defense phase**. Interviewers intentionally stress-test your design by probing edge cases: *'What happens when a database shard dies?' 'How do you handle a viral celebrity tweet?' 'How do you prevent duplicate payments on network timeouts?'* Proactively answering these questions demonstrates production maturity.
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine a Formula 1 race car designer presenting a new car. Phase 1 and 2 showed the aerodynamic body and engine size. Phase 3 and 4 is where the engineer explains: 'Here is the carbon-fiber crash structure for a 200 mph impact (SPOF defense). Here is the dual independent brake hydraulics system (Failover). Here is the telemetry sensor array that adjusts fuel-air mixtures every millisecond (Adaptive Caching & Backpressure).'
topics.how_it_works:
Executing Steps 13 to 21 systematically:

  1. Step 13: Deep Dive into Core Bottleneck: Drill into the hardest technical problem (e.g., Video Transcoding DAG in YouTube, Spatial Grid in Uber, or Timeline Fan-out in Twitter).
  2. Step 14: Data Partitioning (Sharding): Select a high-cardinality Shard Key (e.g., hash(user_id) % N via Consistent Hashing) to distribute data evenly across database nodes.
  3. Step 15: Caching & Invalidation: Define Cache-Aside pattern, set TTL policies (e.g., 2 hours), and resolve Cache Stampedes using Single-Flight / Mutex locks.
  4. Step 16: Concurrency & Race Conditions: Eliminate race conditions using Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC with version numbers) or distributed locks with fencing tokens.
  5. Step 17: Idempotency: Enforce Idempotency-Key headers and Transactional Inbox deduplication tables.
  6. Step 18: Single Point of Failure (SPOF) Removal: Ensure $N+1$ redundancy across all tiers: Multi-AZ load balancers, database primary-standby with automated failover, and multi-broker Kafka clusters.
  7. Step 19: Disaster Recovery & Replication Lag: Address master-slave replication lag using 'Read-Your-Own-Writes' session routing.
  8. Step 20: Master Trade-off Defense: Present a clear comparison matrix justifying your CP vs AP decisions, latency vs consistency compromises, and storage vs compute trade-offs.
  9. Step 21: Conclusion & Future Improvements: Summarize system strengths and propose future optimizations (e.g., ML-based caching, edge compute workers).

conceptual_breakdown.explanation: Update rows using version numbers: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 50, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 101 AND version = 3;`. If zero rows updated, another thread modified state concurrently; retry transaction.
When a hot key expires, thousands of threads miss simultaneously. Use mutex locking so only 1 thread recomputes the cache while others wait, protecting the database.
If a user updates their profile, pin their subsequent reads to the Primary DB for 5 seconds, ensuring they see their own updates while replicas catch up asynchronously.
When cluster CPU exceeds 85%, shed non-critical background jobs (e.g., recommendation feeds) with HTTP 503, preserving 100% capacity for core transactions (checkout/login).

rows: 100% site write downtime until manual reboot
Automated Multi-AZ failover promotes standby replica in <60 seconds
Thundering herd crashes database with 50k QPS
Single-flight mutex locking + probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)
User clicks button 3 times, billed 3 times
Idempotency-Key header + Transactional Inbox deduplication table
User posts photo, refreshes, photo vanishes
Session-based 'Read-Your-Own-Writes' routing to Primary for 5 seconds
One slow downstream service freezes all API threads
Circuit Breaker trips to Open (Fail-Fast in <1ms) + Bulkhead pools

tradeoffs.factor: Multi-AZ Synchronous Standby vs Write Latency
tradeoffs.analysis: Synchronous replication to a standby AZ adds $<1$ms latency but guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) and automated failover (RTO $< 60$s) during a datacenter blackout.

Pessimistic locking (`SELECT FOR UPDATE`) holds database row locks, causing lock convoys under high contention. Optimistic locking (OCC with version column) eliminates lock contention with zero database locking overhead.

failure_scenarios.scenario: Network Partition Isolates 2 out of 5 Consensus Nodes
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Minority partition safely rejects writes to prevent split-brain data corruption; majority 3-node partition continues operating smoothly.

failure_scenarios.scenario: Poison Pill Task Crashes Worker Fleet
failure_scenarios.impact: A malformed task payload crashes worker processes in an infinite retry loop.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Configure a maximum retry cap (e.g., 3 retries) with exponential backoff, moving poison tasks to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) and paging on-call engineers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Claiming a system has zero failure modes
common_mistakes.correction: Every distributed system has failure modes. Always identify your single points of failure proactively and present clear architectural mitigations.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using distributed locking for high-volume transactions without fencing tokens
common_mistakes.correction: Locks expire during JVM GC pauses. Always use monotonic fencing tokens verified at storage level or switch to Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC).

interview_questions.question: How do you defend against the 'Hot Key' (Celebrity) problem in a distributed cache like Redis?
interview_questions.answer: Apply a four-tier defense strategy: (1) **Local In-Memory Cache (L1):** Store hot keys in the API Gateway's local RAM for 5-10 seconds, absorbing 90% of requests before hitting Redis; (2) **Key Splitting / Salt Partitioning:** Partition a hot key across $N$ shards by appending a random integer suffix: `hot_key_0`, `hot_key_1` ... `hot_key_9`. Writes update all 10 keys; reads query `hot_key_random(0,9)`, distributing load across 10 independent Redis instances; (3) **Read Replicas:** Deploy read replicas on the Redis master shard; (4) **CDN Edge Caching:** For static/semi-static content, cache the object at Cloudflare/CloudFront edge PoPs.

interview_questions.question: What is the 'Read-Your-Own-Writes' consistency challenge, and how do you solve it in master-slave database architectures?
interview_questions.answer: When a user executes a write (e.g., updating their bio), the write commits to the Primary database. The primary replicates the write asynchronously to Read Replicas with a 50-200ms replication lag. If the user immediately refreshes the page and their read is routed to a lagging replica, they see their old bio and assume the update failed. Mitigation: (1) **Session-based Tracking:** Set a cookie or JWT timestamp `last_write_timestamp = NOW()`. If `NOW() - last_write_timestamp < 5 seconds`, force the read query to execute on the Primary database; (2) **Replication Coordinates:** Store the commit LSN (Log Sequence Number) in the session cookie and ensure the replica has replayed past that LSN before executing the query.
